reviews.review:
Northwind does something completely different with its core gameplay compared to most entries in the genre, leading to a very unique experience. The biggest divergences from most other games in the genre are as follows:

 - Most of the resources (e.g. mana, block, many status effects) persist from one turn to the next
 - Mana is generated by drawing specific resource generating cards rather than you gaining a fixed amount each turn
 - There's a level up mechanic where you can expend mana to power up most of your cards for the rest of the fight
 - Your attack and defense are fundamentally one and the same, with your accumulated attack value for the turn being compared against the enemy's to determine who takes damage and how much (block, mentioned earlier, is more of a long term defensive mechanic that isn't nearly as easy to get as it is in a lot of games in the genre).

All of this makes the battles somewhat slower, with a distinct early, middle and late game and a corresponding focus on long term planning and resource management. Due to this, most battles feel winnable with proper decision making and defeats feel like a consequence of bad resource management or a poorly constructed deck (which can, admittedly, be thanks to a poor selection of cards to draft, like in any deckbuilder). 

Besides all of this, they've done a number of changes to the surrounding gameplay systems, which serve to either improve on some genre staples or, at the very least, change up the formula:

- Consumables have been replaced with perks, which are generally slightly less powerful but can be reused each battle. No more dying while trying to save the potion for a later battle.
- Each act is shorter, usually consisting of three to four enemy encounters and three to four other events (this is pretty important since each fight takes longer due to how combat works).
- The map for each act has been streamlined considerably, so that instead of trying to plan a route through the entire act at the start you are essentially choosing from a series of forks.
- Most card upgrading is done in a between act town area, with a gem socketing system that allows for a lot of flexibility in how you empower your cards.
- Instead of getting a random boss each act from a pool for that act, each run you fight a progressively harder version of the boss you select in act 1. This has its pros and cons, but I personally find it satisfying being able to tailor my build to be able to deal with the monster I'm hunting down for the run.

As far as the amount of content in the game goes, as of this writing there are currently two characters that play quite differently from each other. They both have several distinct builds that can work and, taken together with the gem socketing mentioned earlier, I rarely feel like I'm doing the same thing from one run to the next.

All that being said, the game isn't without its flaws, most of which come down to balance or performance and will hopefully be fixed through early access. Notably:
- Enemy encounters vary wildly in difficulty. Some normal encounters feel harder than most of the elite encounters and some elite encounters feel harder than a lot of the bosses.
- If you get a REALLY big deck (maybe 40-50 cards?) the game slows down any time you need to shuffle/look through it.
- While perks and gems are broken up into two different tiers, even within a tier there's a lot of variation in how strong they are, with some upgrades feeling borderline useless compared to others.
- You can fuse duplicates of cards together to ostensibly make them more powerful, but many of these "upgrades" feel more like...sidegrades, or sometimes even downgrades.
- There's currently no inspection feature for the cards, meaning you don't know what the fused version will look like until you actually go to do it (worth noting that they explicitly list an inspection feature as something they'll be adding in their roadmap, so I expect this will be fixed later).

All in all, if you like roguelike deckbuilders, or have been wanting to give them a try, and are looking for something different, I strongly recommend Northwind.
